question: In December 2023 and February 2024, the Commission sent two letters to the Slovakian Government expressing its concern over its proposed reforms aimed at: (i) abolishing the special prosecutor’s office; and (ii) reducing penalties for corruption offences.

The Commission argued that these reforms could compromise the protection of the EU’s financial interests by weakening defences against the illicit use of public funds. It called for the reforms to be suspended and warned the Slovakian Government that its EU funding could be affected if they went ahead. 1.

Spain’s Organic Law 14/2022 of 23 December amended its Penal Code to reduce the penalties for misappropriation of public funds, thereby undermining the Union’s financial interests, just as Slovakia is doing. So why did the Commission not ask Spain to put that law on hold?

Will it ask Spain to abolish that reform and restore the penalties for misappropriation? Will it warn Spain of the potential repercussions of non-compliance, as it did in its letters to the Slovakian Government?
answer: The EU is competent to adopt directives to harmonise the definition of, and penalties for, criminal offences listed in Article 83(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU or concerning the effective implementation of a Union policy in an area which has been subject to harmonisation measures.
With respect to other criminal offences, Member States remain free to adopt or amend legislation as they deem appropriate, as long as they respect their obligations under international and EU law.

Pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2017/1371 (‘PIF Directive’) (1), Member States have to take the necessary measures to ensure that misappropriation of funds or assets, in any way which damages the EU’s financial interests, constitutes a criminal offence when committed intentionally.

This should be read in conjunction with Article 7 of the directive, which requires Member States to ensure effective, proportionate and dissuasive criminal sanctions for the criminal offences covered by the directive, including a maximum penalty of at least four years of imprisonment when these offences involve considerable damage or advantage (i.e. damage or advantage of more than EUR 100 000).

The Commission is aware that, further to the adoption of the Spanish Organic Law 14/2022, penalty thresholds for some cases of misappropriation have been lowered. The 2023 Country Chapter on the rule of law situation in Spain duly acknowledges these developments (2).

The Commission is assessing the compliance of the above-mentioned Law with the PIF Directive and contacted the Spanish authorities for further clarifications. As with other Member States, the Commission is ready to take appropriate measures to ensure compliance with EU law, as necessary.

Directive (EU) 2017/1371 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 July 2017 on the fight against fraud to the Union's financial interests by means of criminal law, OJ L 198, 28.7.2017, p. 29-41. 2023 Rule of Law Report Country. Chapter on the rule of law situation in Spain, SWD(2023) 809 final, pp. 13-14, available here: https://eurlex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:52023SC0809
